extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators (and philosophers of mathematical practice) seeking an accessible survey of themes and methods in the philosophy of mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: A survey article aimed at mathematics educators that (1) describes the core questions philosophers of mathematical practice investigate and the philosophical methods they use, and (2) gives a selective overview of topics such as the formal/informal proof distinction, visualization and artefacts, mathematical explanation and understanding, value judgments, and mathematical design, with remarks on connections to mathematics education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between formal and informal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper highlights the distinction between formal and informal proofs as a central topic in the philosophy of mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses differences and challenges raised by each type (references: Hamami (2018) for analysis of differences; Hamami (forthcoming) for attempts to meet challenges compatible with the standard view). This dimension invites evaluating proofs by whether they are wholly formalizable, how informal reasoning relies on conventions or 'acceptable gaps', and what epistemic roles informal proofs play in mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization and artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualization and artefacts (e.g., diagrams, pictures) are identified as a core theme: how visual representations contribute to mathematical reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys work on visual and diagrammatic thinking (references: Giaquinto 2016; Giardino 2017a; Miller 2007; Mumma 2006, 2010; Avigad, Dean, & Mumma 2009; Panza 2012). Guidance includes assessing when diagrams are epistemically reliable, the relation between geometric objects and their diagrams, and attempts to formalize diagrammatic reasoning. For educators, this involves judging appropriate uses of visualization in teaching and when to require formal backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical explanation and understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical explanation and understanding is treated as a distinct evaluative dimension: what makes a proof/explanation explanatory and how understanding is achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers varieties of mathematical explanation and debates about explanatory proofs (references: Hafner & Mancosu; Lange; D'Alessandro; Fraser). Includes issues such as unity, symmetry, salience, mechanistic explanation, and instrumental value of explanations (see Morris forthcoming). Use this to evaluate proofs and pedagogical choices by their explanatory power and capacity to foster understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value judgments in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper identifies 'value judgments' (aesthetic, pragmatic, and epistemic values such as beauty, fruitfulness) as part of mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References work on mathematical beauty, fruitfulness, and aesthetics (Rota 1997; Sinclair 2004; Tappenden 2012; Lange 2016). Guidance: consider how non-epistemic and epistemic values influence appraisal of proofs, results, and methods, and how these judgments bear on teaching priorities and curriculum design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical design
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical design is listed among the topics surveyed—concerned with how mathematical objects, proofs, and representations are constructed or engineered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although briefly noted in the abstract, this dimension covers choices in definitions, representations, and structuring of arguments. For educators, it bears on how tasks, examples, and proofs are designed to achieve pedagogical goals; the paper signals this as an area connecting practice to pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core questions and philosophical methods in the philosophy of mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors describe the core questions philosophers of mathematical practice investigate and the philosophical methods they use to tackle them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include historical case studies, conceptual analysis, formal reconstruction, empirical/experimental approaches, and sociological perspectives (the paper surveys these approaches). Use this to evaluate research or teaching interventions by the appropriateness of method to the question (e.g., when an empirical study of mathematicians' behavior is required versus conceptual analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal logic of mathematical proof and acceptable gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: The informal logic of proofs and the notion of acceptable gaps in mathematical proofs are highlighted as topics of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References include Aberdein (2006) on informal logic and Andersen (forthcoming) on acceptable gaps. Guidance: evaluate mathematical arguments with attention to conventions about acceptable omissions, how gaps are justified within disciplinary practice, and implications for rigor in teaching and assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of peer review and testimony in mathematical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of peer review and knowledge by testimony in mathematics is presented as a sociological/epistemic dimension of practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites work on peer review and testimony (Geist, Löwe, & Van Kerkhove 2010). Use this to assess how communal practices, trust, and testimonial transmission contribute to validation of results and to decisions about what to teach or accept as established knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded but relevant themes: computers in mathematical inquiry and ethics in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors explicitly note two important themes they do not address in this paper: the role of computers in mathematical inquiry and ethics in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although excluded from this primer, these are flagged as relevant evaluative dimensions elsewhere (references: Avigad 2008a for computers; Rogers & Kaiser 1995; Ernest 2016, 2018; Rittberg et al. forthcoming for ethics). For educators and evaluators, this entry serves as a reminder to consider computational methods and ethical implications when assessing contemporary mathematical practice.
